---
title: "What your QA produces, and who owns it"
order: 28
---

## The ticket

Monday morning, five things are waiting from your Quality Analyst (QA), all routed within the
same hour.

1. A deviation packet — a shipping-cooler temperature excursion caught on a routine audit,
   nothing shipped out of range, contained the same day — with a signature line on the last
   page: "Final disposition approval: ______." A sticky note on top says "needs your sign-off
   before I can close it."
2. The validation impact assessment for last month's BECS (Blood Establishment Computer
   Software) operating-system patch — the one she rejected outright until someone wrote this
   down — routed to you "for approval."
3. The annual reassessment of one of Lakeshore's reagent suppliers, due this quarter, routed
   "for sign-off."
4. A one-line message: a night-shift supervisor asked her whether she should call you at 2 a.m.
   if something similar happens again this week, and she wants to know what you want her to
   tell him.
5. A first draft of next quarter's management-review packet, for you to skim before she
   finalizes it.

Five documents, five requests to put your name on something, all landing before your coffee's
finished. You start with the deviation packet, because it's shortest. You're two words into
signing "Final disposition approval" when something stops you: you don't actually know what
disposition authority means at Lakeshore, or whether it's yours to give.

It isn't. Every deviation you've seen her close — going back to the Owen Pruitt donation and
the Brookfield binder — named "the medical director or a delegated quality officer" as the
person who decides what happens to the product. Not you. Not IT. You almost signed a box that
was never built for your name.

You put the pen down and look at the other four items differently. The patch assessment wants
your approval too — but you *are* supposed to be in that box, as the system's owner, the way
the change-control lesson from `quality-system-essentials` already established. The vendor
reassessment wants a "sign-off" you're not sure is the same kind of act as either of the first
two. The 2 a.m. question isn't asking you to sign anything at all. And the management-review
draft doesn't want your signature — it wants you to have read it before Thursday.

Five requests, four different things "your name on this" actually means, and you only caught
the one that mattered because you happened to read the label on the box before your hand moved.
That's the gap this lesson closes.

## Why this matters — and the ITIL bridge

You already do a version of this every week. A change ticket lands in your queue and you know,
without being told, whether you're the implementer, the approver, or just a name on the
notification list — that's RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, informed), the framework
that keeps one person from silently owning three different roles on the same piece of work. A
CAB (change advisory board) approval means something specific too: you're attesting the change
is safe to deploy from a service-risk read, not that you personally verified every line the
engineer wrote.

Your QA's deliverables ask you to run that same RACI discipline, except the roles now carry
regulatory weight, and one of the boxes was never built for someone in IT's reporting line to
sign at all. The failure mode this lesson exists to prevent isn't a bad decision — it's a
**misattributed** one. A signature in the wrong box doesn't just look sloppy to an assessor; it
reads as evidence that nobody at Lakeshore actually knows who's accountable for what, which
calls every other signature in the building into question at once.

There's a second concept you already own that applies here with more teeth than usual:
**separation of duties (SoD)**. You've lived this under SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley, the law that
requires financial controls be split so no one person can both initiate and approve the same
transaction) — the person who cuts a purchase order can't also approve it, even if they're
honest, because the control protects the *system* from a single point of failure, not because
anyone's assumed dishonest. Your QA's independence on quality decisions is the same control in
different clothes: she has to be free to reach a disposition, a reportability call, or a "this
change isn't validated yet" rejection that your IT priorities would rather not hear, and the
control only works if nothing about the reporting line quietly erodes it — more on exactly what
this does and doesn't require below.

Where the blood-industry version demands more than your IT world usually does: a signature on a
regulated record isn't a soft approval you can walk back with "I glanced at it and it looked
fine." It's an accountable, attributable act — the kind an inspector reads as a claim you made,
personally, about what you verified. "I didn't really look" is not a defense once your name is
on the line; it's the finding.

## The rule in plain English

**What your QA actually produces.** No two blood centers structure this identically, so treat
what follows as **typical, not a fixed list** — confirm the actual map against Lakeshore's own
org chart and SOPs before you rely on it. At most blood centers, a Quality Analyst's output
clusters into eight kinds of work:

- Deviation and CAPA (corrective and preventive action) records
- Change-control quality reviews and impact assessments
- Validation impact assessments for systems like BECS
- Document-control work (drafting, reviewing, and retiring controlled procedures)
- Supplier and vendor assessments
- Participation in internal and external audits
- Inputs to management review
- Support during an inspection or assessment (pulling records, answering an investigator's
  questions)

**Three kinds of review sit on top of that list, and they belong to different people:**

1. **Supervisory review — yours.** Is the write-up defensible, complete, internally
   consistent, and consistent with what IT independently knows? Does it show its reasoning? Is
   it her best work? This is the review a good manager runs on any direct report's output, aimed
   at a document instead of a postmortem.
2. **Quality approval — Quality leadership or the medical director, per Lakeshore's own SOPs.**
   Is the *quality decision* itself right — disposition, reportability, release?
3. **Independent assessment — internal audit, AABB, or FDA.** Does practice actually match the
   paper, checked by someone with no stake in either answer?

You own #1 on everything she writes. You never own #2 — that's the line the deviation packet
almost made you cross. And #3 isn't yours to perform at all; it's the outside check on whether
#1 and #2 were done honestly.

**What your signature attests to changes with the box you're in**, and there are three
possibilities:

- **Supervisor.** Your name means "I reviewed this, it's defensible, and I'd stand behind it if
  someone asked me about it cold." It does not mean you agree with — or have the authority to
  make — the underlying quality call.
- **System-owner co-approver.** On BECS and other IT/validated-system changes, `becs-in-the-
  pipeline` and the change-control lesson already established that you're a *named* approver
  alongside Quality, as the system's owner — "both required, neither sufficient alone." Here your
  signature means something closer to Quality's: a real, substantive approval, not a courtesy.
  This is the box the patch assessment belongs in.
- **Informed.** No signature at all — you're on the notification list because you need to know,
  not because anyone needs your consent. The management-review draft and most document-control
  routine work land here.

**Delegation's static half** — the part that doesn't move with her track record, as opposed to
the part that widens over time as she earns it (a later module's job):

- **Her decisions alone.** Routine, well-precedented calls: closing a low-severity deviation
  with a documented cause statement and no CAPA, minor document revisions that don't touch a
  controlled process, day-to-day audit-participation logistics.
- **Your concurrence required.** Anything where you're a named system-owner co-approver — BECS
  and validated-system changes, IT vendor decisions with a quality dimension.
- **Decisions that stay with you regardless.** Whether a document is ready to leave your desk
  under your name at all — that supervisory sign-off can't be delegated back to her, because it's
  a check *on* her work, not a task she performs — and the call to escalate something above both
  of you.

**Protecting her independence isn't a regulatory requirement you can cite — be precise about
that.** There's no FDA regulation in this curriculum's sources that requires quality decisions to
sit outside an IT reporting line, and this lesson won't invent one. What's real is the SoD
principle from the ITIL bridge above, plus a fact you can act on directly: Lakeshore's own SOPs
already name who holds disposition and quality-approval authority, and it isn't you. Treat that
as the boundary. Your job is making sure nothing about "she reports to me" quietly pressures a
quality call — never rushing a disposition to hit a change-freeze date, never treating a rejected
patch as a performance issue. You coach the quality of her write-ups. You never coach the outcome
of her quality decisions.

**The shared instrument you'll use on all of it: the cold-read test.** Every document she hands
you, whatever kind it is, gets the same question: *would this survive an inspector reading it
cold, a year from now, with her not in the room?* Six questions do the work, and they're worth
memorizing by name, because every later module in this course applies them by these exact
labels:

1. **Conclusion.** What does this document decide? Is there exactly one, stated plainly?
2. **Evidence.** What objective evidence supports it — attached or retrievable — and does it
   cover the *whole* claim?
3. **Reasoning.** Is the path from evidence to conclusion written down, or only the answer?
4. **Criteria first.** Was the bar — acceptance criterion, effectiveness criterion, risk tier —
   set *before* the result was known?
5. **Decision trail.** Who decided, with what authority, and in what order — do the dates show
   assessment before approval before implementation?
6. **Loose ends.** Is every open item owned and dated? Is anything marked "closed" while it still
   depends on something "TBD"?

This is this course's own synthesis of what you've already been taught to look for — QSE's
"what an inspector would actually look for" sections, its effectiveness-check discipline, its
insistence on a written reportability determination — collected into one habit instead of three
separate checklists. It isn't an AABB checklist or an FDA form. No citation attaches to it because
none exists; label it industry practice, or just call it what it is: how you read.

Once the cold-read test finds something, it needs a bucket, not a red pen through everything at
once. **Gap triage** sorts every finding into one of three categories:

- **Must fix before I sign** — the document is indefensible without it.
- **Fix going forward** — a real weakness that doesn't undermine *this* conclusion.
- **Fine as is** — looks odd, isn't actually wrong.

That third category matters as much as the first. A director who red-pens everything trains a
QA to write defensively, padding every document against imagined objections, instead of writing
clearly. Not every rough edge is a gap.

**A quick worked example**, small enough to run in thirty seconds, before you ever try this on a
full document — that's module 2's job, not this one. The foundation lesson on risk vocabulary
showed a deviation closed with exactly one line: *"Closed — no patient impact."* Run the six
questions against it. Conclusion: there is one, and it's stated (no patient impact). Evidence:
none attached — nothing shows what was checked. Reasoning: absent entirely; the line states an
outcome, not a path to it. Criteria first: no criterion is named at all. Decision trail: no
author, no date, no authority shown. Loose ends: unknowable, because nothing else is written.
Triage verdict: **must fix before I sign** — not because the conclusion is probably wrong (it
might well be right), but because nothing on the page lets anyone but the person who wrote it
believe it.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 11.10(j) | "Eleven point ten, paragraph j" | Written policies holding individuals accountable and responsible for actions taken under their electronic signatures, to deter falsification. | The regulatory grounding for "your signature means something specific" — it doesn't just mean "sign here," it means Lakeshore has to be able to hold you to whatever the box you signed actually claims. |
| 21 CFR 606.100(c) | "Six-oh-six point one-hundred, paragraph c" | First sentence: product records reviewed before release or distribution. Second sentence: a thorough, documented investigation of any discrepancy. | The contrast behind this module's regulatory-requirement question below — a real record-review requirement exists, but it's product-record review, not your supervisory review of her write-up. |
| 21 CFR 606.160(b)(7)(iii) | "Six-oh-six point one-sixty, paragraph b, sub-seven, clause iii" | Biological product deviations must be kept among an establishment's general records. | The reason a deviation record exists at all for you to review — the regulation requires the record; Lakeshore's own SOP decides who signs the disposition box on it. |
| 21 CFR 606.20(b) | "Six-oh-six point twenty, paragraph b" | Personnel performing collection, processing, testing, storage, or distribution steps must be adequate in number, training, and experience, with "a thorough understanding of the procedures or control operations they perform." | The regulatory floor under the question "is she qualified to write what she's writing" — worth having in your pocket before you ever coach a gap in her competence, not her judgment. |

## The actual text

Your signature's accountability, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/11.10.md`:

> (j) The establishment of, and adherence to, written policies that hold individuals accountable
> and responsible for actions initiated under their electronic signatures, in order to deter
> record and signature falsification.

That's a policy requirement, not a description of what any one signature must mean — Lakeshore
decides that, box by box, in its own SOPs. What the regulation actually demands is that whatever
Lakeshore decides, it's written down and enforced, so "I signed it but didn't really mean
anything by it" isn't an available defense once a policy exists.

The contrast at the center of this module, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.100.md`:

> All records pertinent to the lot or unit maintained pursuant to these regulations shall be
> reviewed before the release or distribution of a lot or unit of final product. The review or
> portions of the review may be performed at appropriate periods during or after blood
> collecting, processing, compatibility testing and storing. A thorough investigation, including
> the conclusions and followup, of any unexplained discrepancy or the failure of a lot or unit to
> meet any of its specifications shall be made and recorded.

Read the first sentence carefully: it *does* require record review before a unit is released —
but that's a review of the *product's* records, by whoever Lakeshore's SOP assigns to release
authority, performed as part of getting the unit out the door. It is not a requirement that a
Director review, let alone approve, the deviation write-up that documents an investigation after
the fact. Those are two different reviews, on two different clocks, and conflating them is
exactly how you'd have ended up signing a box the SOP never gave you.

The record requirement behind the deviation packet itself, quoted verbatim from
`sources/cfr/606.160.md`:

> (7) General records: ... (iii) Biological product deviations.

And the competence floor, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.20.md`:

> (b) The personnel responsible for the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage or
> distribution of blood or blood components shall be adequate in number, educational background,
> training and experience... to assure competent performance of their assigned functions... All
> personnel shall have capabilities commensurate with their assigned functions, a thorough
> understanding of the procedures or control operations they perform, the necessary training or
> experience, and adequate information concerning the application of pertinent provisions of this
> part to their respective functions.

AABB's Quality System Essentials (QSE) framework builds directly on top of that floor — no
standard number, paraphrased only, from `sources/aabb/qse-framework.md`: **Organization** (QSE 1)
covers executive management's responsibility and authority, including who can approve exceptions
to policy — the theme behind why a disposition box belongs to someone specific — and
**Resources** (QSE 2) covers job qualifications, competence assessment, and training — the theme
behind 606.20(b) above, formalized into an ongoing program rather than a one-time hiring bar.

## What an inspector or assessor would actually look for

An assessor reading Lakeshore's deviation, change, and validation files doesn't ask "did the
Director sign this." They ask a sharper question: **does the signature on this line match the
authority Lakeshore's own SOP assigns to that line?** A disposition box signed by an IT director
instead of the named quality authority is a finding on its own, independent of whether the
disposition itself was correct — it reads as a quality system that doesn't actually control who
decides what.

They'll also look for **evidence your review happened at all**, not just that it happened
correctly — comments, questions back to the author, a dated mark distinguishing "reviewed" from
"received." A review that leaves no trace is functionally invisible to someone reading the file
later. And on independence specifically, an assessor watching a QA who reports through IT will
look for whether she has ever actually rejected or delayed something IT wanted — a patch, a
change window, a go-live date — and whether that rejection survived without being quietly
overridden through the reporting line. One instance of independence exercised and respected is
worth more than any policy statement about it.

## Common traps

**"My signature always means the same thing."** It doesn't, and this module exists because that
assumption is exactly what almost got a disposition signed in the wrong box. Supervisor,
system-owner co-approver, and informed are three different acts, and the only way to avoid
signing the wrong one is to ask which box you're in before your hand moves, every time — not to
assume consistency that isn't actually there.

**"She reports to me, so FDA requires me to sign off on her quality decisions" — or its mirror,
"since she reports to me, her independence is really just a courtesy I extend."** Both are wrong,
and both are versions of the same regulatory-requirement question worth asking directly: **does
FDA require the Director to approve every deviation record?** No. Who approves a disposition is
Lakeshore's own SOP choice, not a federal mandate — what the regulation actually requires is the
investigation and its record (606.100(c), 606.160(b)(7)(iii)), not any particular person's
signature on it. That cuts both ways: you can't claim FDA forces your hand onto the disposition
line, and you can't wave away her independence as optional because no regulation in this
curriculum's sources spells it out as a citable requirement either. What holds her independence in
place is the separation-of-duties principle and Lakeshore's own SOP naming someone else for that
box — real, but not the kind of thing you cite chapter and verse to an inspector.

## What this means for your job

- **Before you sign anything, name the box out loud: supervisor, system-owner co-approver, or
  informed.** If you can't say which one in one sentence, don't sign yet — go find out.
- **Learn Lakeshore's own SOP-named authorities for disposition and quality approval before you
  need them under pressure.** The Monday stack almost turned into a finding because that knowledge
  wasn't already reflexive.
- **Run the cold-read test on anything before you sign it, not just the documents that feel
  weighty.** Conclusion, Evidence, Reasoning, Criteria first, Decision trail, Loose ends — six
  questions, thirty seconds on something small, longer on something that matters.
- **Sort every finding with gap triage before you say anything to her: must fix before I sign, fix
  going forward, or fine as is.** Sending back a document with every line marked "must fix" teaches
  defensive writing, not better writing.
- **Protect her independence as a daily habit, not a policy you filed once.** Never let a
  deadline, a change freeze, or a go-live date become the reason a quality call gets rushed.

One line on what this module doesn't cover: exactly which events have to reach you, and how fast,
is module 3's job. For now, just know the map exists.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA routes a deviation packet to you "for approval," with a disposition signature line on the last page. What's the right move?

Check Lakeshore's own SOP for who holds disposition authority before you sign anything. In this
curriculum, that authority has consistently been named as the medical director or a delegated
quality officer — not the IT Director, even though the QA reports to him. Your legitimate role on
this document is supervisory review: is it defensible, complete, and does it show its reasoning?
That's a real review worth doing carefully. It just isn't the same act as disposition approval,
and routing habits (a form that's always gone to "the boss") can put your name on a line that was
never built for it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: "FDA requires the Director to approve every deviation record before it can close." True or false?

False. Nothing in this curriculum's sources — 606.100(c) or 606.160(b)(7)(iii) — names who at a
blood establishment must sign a deviation's disposition. What's actually required is the
investigation itself, made and recorded, and the record's existence among the establishment's
general records. *Who* signs which box is Lakeshore's own SOP choice. Worth noting the flip side
in the same breath: 606.100(c)'s first sentence does require product records to be reviewed
before release — a real, regulation-tier requirement — but that's a different review, on a
different clock, performed by whoever holds release authority, not your supervisory read of the
deviation write-up after the fact.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: A one-paragraph closure note reads only "Closed — no patient impact." Using gap triage, is this fine as is, fix going forward, or must fix before you sign?

Must fix before you sign. Running the cold-read test on it: there's a conclusion, but no
evidence, no reasoning, no stated criterion, and no visible decision trail — nothing on the page
would let a stranger reach the same conclusion, whether or not the conclusion itself happens to be
correct. That's not a stylistic nitpick you can defer to "fix going forward"; a document this thin
can't be defended if someone asks about it a year from now, which is the whole point of the test.
:::

## Where this goes next

You now have the map: what she typically produces, who writes it, who approves it, who's merely
informed, what your own signature means in each role, and one instrument — the cold-read test,
plus gap triage — for reading any of it. The next module, `reviewing-deviations-and-capas`, is
where you actually use that instrument on a real, complete document: a full deviation and CAPA
packet, planted gaps and all, read the way an assessor would read it cold.
